cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK V
Calypso's island: the raft, Poseidon's storm, the landing on Scheria.
And Dawn rose from her bed beside lordly Tithonus\nto carry light to the immortals and to mortals;
and the gods were sitting down in council, among them\nZeus who thunders on high, whose power is greatest.
And Athena was telling over the many cares of Odysseus,
remembering: it galled her that\nhe was still in the nymph's house:
"Father Zeus, and you other blessed gods who are forever:
let no sceptered king ever again be willingly kind\nand gentle, or know the right way in his heart;
let him rather be harsh always, and act outrage —\nsince no one remembers godlike Odysseus
among the people he ruled, and he was gentle as a father.
No — he lies on an island suffering strong pains in\nthe halls of the nymph Calypso, who holds him there
by force; and he cannot come to his own fatherland,\nfor he has no ships at hand, no oars, no companions
to carry him over the broad back of the sea.
And now, besides, men are bent on killing his beloved\nson on his way home: he went for news of his father
to holy Pylos and to shining Lacedaemon."
Then Zeus who gathers the clouds answered her:
"My child, what a word has\nslipped the fence of your teeth!
Was it not you who framed this plan yourself —
that Odysseus should come home\nand take vengeance on those men?
As for Telemachus: guide him with\nyour skill — you have the power —
so that he reaches his own fatherland untouched,\nand the suitors come back in their ship with nothing done."
He spoke, and turned to Hermes, his dear son:
"Hermes — you are our messenger in all things else:
tell the nymph of the lovely braids our fixed decree:
the homecoming of enduring-hearted\nOdysseus — that he shall return
with no escort of gods and none of mortal men:
on a raft bound plank to plank, and suffering pains,
on the twentieth day he shall reach rich-soiled Scheria,
the land of the Phaeacians,\nwho are born close kin to the gods.
They will honor him with all their hearts, like a god,\nand send him in a ship to his own dear fatherland,
giving him bronze and gold and clothing in plenty,\nmore than Odysseus would ever have carried out of Troy
had he come home untouched with\nhis fair share of the spoils.
For so it is his portion: to see his own people and\ncome to his high-roofed house and his own fatherland."
So he spoke, and the guide,\nthe slayer of Argus, did not disobey.
At once he bound beneath his feet the beautiful sandals,\nambrosial, golden, that carry him over the water
and over the boundless earth with the breath of the wind;
and he took up the rod with which he charms men's eyes
to sleep, whose eyes he wills,\nand wakes others from their slumber.
With this in his hands the strong slayer of Argus flew.
He stepped down on Pieria,\nthen dropped from the high air to the sea
and skimmed along the waves like a shearwater,\nthe bird that down the terrible troughs of the barren sea
hunts fish, and wets its beating wings in the brine:
like that bird Hermes rode the crowding waves.
But when he reached the island, far away,\nhe stepped from the violet sea onto dry land
and went on till he came to the great cave where the nymph
of the lovely braids was living; he found her within.
A great fire was burning on the hearth, and the smell\nof split cedar and citron-wood burning carried far,
all over the island. Inside,\nshe was singing in a beautiful voice,
moving to and fro at the loom,\nweaving with a golden shuttle.
And around the cave a wood grew tall and flourishing:
alder and black poplar and sweet-smelling cypress,\nwhere long-winged birds made their roosts,
little owls and hawks and long-tongued crows\nof the sea, whose business is the waters.
And there, trained over the hollow of the cave,\nspread a garden vine in its prime, heavy with clusters;
and four springs in a row ran with bright water,\nclose by one another, turned each its own way;
and around them soft meadows of violet and wild celery\nwere blooming. There even a deathless one, arriving,
would gaze in wonder at the\nsight and be gladdened at heart.
There the guide, the slayer of Argus, stood gazing.
And when his heart had wondered at it all,\nhe went straight into the wide cave. Nor did Calypso,
shining among goddesses, fail to know him face to face:
for the deathless gods are not unknown to one another,\nnot even one whose dwelling lies far off.
But great-hearted Odysseus he did not find within:
he sat weeping on the shore, where he always sat,\nshredding his heart with tears and groans and pains,
and over the barren sea he would gaze,\nletting the tears run.
And Calypso, shining among goddesses, questioned Hermes,\nseating him on a chair all bright and gleaming:
"Why have you come to me, Hermes of the golden rod,
honored guest and dear?\nYou have not been used to come before.
Say what is in your mind: my heart bids me do it\nif I can do it — if it is a thing that can be done.
But follow me in first, and let me set out guest-fare."
So speaking the goddess drew up a table for him,\nheaping it with ambrosia, and mixed the red nectar;
and the guide, the slayer of Argus, drank and ate.
And when he had supped, and steadied his heart with food,\nthen he spoke out in answer to her question:
"You ask me why I come — goddess to god; and I will\ntell you the whole of it truly, since you bid me.
Zeus ordered me here. I did not want to come:
who would choose to cross so vast a stretch of salt water,
past speaking? And no city of mortals near,\nto offer the gods their victims and their choice hecatombs.
But there is no way for another god to slip past\nor thwart the mind of Zeus who bears the aegis.
He says there is a man with you —\nthe most miserable of all
the men who fought nine years around the city of Priam\nand in the tenth year sacked it, and turned for home.
But on the way home they sinned against Athena,\nand she roused an evil wind against them, and long seas.
There all the rest of his brave companions\nperished, but wind and wave carried him here.
That man Zeus bids you send on his way — and quickly:
it is not his portion to die here,\nfar from his own people;
it is still his portion to see his own people and\ncome to his high-roofed house and his own fatherland."
So he spoke; and Calypso,\nshining among goddesses, shivered,
and lifting her voice she spoke winged words to him:
"You are merciless, you gods — jealous beyond all beings —\nwho begrudge goddesses their sleeping with men
openly, if one takes a man as her own dear husband.
So when Dawn of the rose-red fingers took Orion,\nyou gods who live at ease begrudged it to her,
until in Ortygia chaste Artemis of the golden throne\ncame at him with her gentle arrows and killed him.
So when Demeter of the lovely braids gave way to\nher heart and lay with Iasion in love in the bed
of a thrice-plowed fallow field — Zeus was not long
in hearing, and he killed him with\na hurl of the white lightning.
And so now me, you gods:\nyou begrudge me a mortal man beside me.
I saved him — riding astride his keel, alone,\nafter Zeus with a hurl of the white lightning had shattered
his fast ship apart in the middle of the wine-dark sea.
There all the rest of his brave companions\nperished, but wind and wave carried him here.
And I loved him, and I fed him, and I promised\nto make him deathless and unaging all his days.
But since there is no way for another god to slip\npast or thwart the mind of Zeus who bears the aegis —
let him go, if that one urges it and commands,\nout over the barren sea. Only I will not convey him:
I have no ships at hand, no oars, no companions\nto carry him over the broad back of the sea.
But with a willing heart I will\ncounsel him, and hide nothing,
so that he may reach his own fatherland untouched."
Then the guide, the slayer of Argus, answered her:
"Send him so, then — and beware the wrath of Zeus:
let him not turn against you\nafterward and bear hard on you."
So speaking, the strong slayer of Argus went away.
And the queenly nymph went to great-hearted Odysseus,\nnow that she had heard the message of Zeus.
She found him sitting on the shore. His eyes were\nnever dry of tears; his sweet life was draining away
in mourning for his homecoming —\nthe nymph no longer pleased him.
True, at night he would sleep beside her — he had to —
in the hollow caves, unwilling man by willing goddess;
but all his days he sat out on the rocks and the beaches,
shredding his heart with tears and groans and pains,
and over the barren sea he would gaze,\nletting the tears run.
Standing near him, she spoke, shining among goddesses:
"Luckless man, do not sit grieving\nhere any longer; do not let
your life waste away. I am ready now —\nwholly — to send you off.
Come: cut long timbers, and join with bronze\na wide raft; and fix an upper half-deck to it,
raised high, to carry you over the misted sea.
And I will put in bread and water and red wine\nto your heart's content, to keep hunger from you,
and I will clothe you, and send a fair wind behind you,
so that you may reach your own fatherland untouched —\nif the gods are willing, who hold wide heaven,
who are stronger than I to purpose and accomplish."
So she spoke; and much-enduring noble Odysseus shuddered,
and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
"Something else you are plotting here,\ngoddess — not my sending —
you who bid me cross the great gulf of the sea on a raft,
that terror, that misery: not even the trim fast-running
ships cross it, for all their joy in the wind of Zeus.
I will not set foot on any raft against your will —
not unless you bring yourself,\ngoddess, to swear me the great oath
that you are not planning some new evil against me."
So he spoke; and Calypso, shining among goddesses, smiled,
and stroked him with her hand,\nand spoke a word, and named him:
"You are a rogue indeed — no lightweight in cunning —\nto have thought of a speech like that to say to me.
Now let Earth be witness, and the wide Heaven above,\nand the down-dripping water of Styx — the greatest oath
and the most terrible the blessed gods can swear —\nthat I am not planning some new evil against you.
No: I am thinking and advising exactly what I would\ndevise for my own self, if such need came on me.
My mind is honest through and through, and the heart\nin my breast is not made of iron. It knows pity."
So speaking she led the way, shining among goddesses,\nswiftly, and he followed in the footsteps of the god.
They came to the hollow cave, the goddess and the man,\nand he sat down there on the chair from which Hermes
had risen, and the nymph set out\nall manner of food beside him,
to eat and drink, such things as mortal men eat;\nand she took her seat facing godlike Odysseus,
and slave-women set ambrosia and nectar beside her.
And their hands went out to the\ngood things spread before them.
But when they had had their joy of food and drink,\nCalypso began, shining among goddesses:
"Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices —
so you would go home now, home to your own dear country,
at once, this moment? Go, then —\nand joy go with you even so.
But if you knew in your heart how full your measure\nof sorrow is before you reach your own country,
you would stay here with me and keep this house,\nand be deathless — for all your longing to see
that wife of yours, whom you ache for all your days.
And yet I dare say I am not beneath her —\nnot in form, not in stature: it is in no way seemly
for mortal women to vie with immortals in body and looks."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Goddess and queen, do not be angry\nwith me for this. I know it all
myself, well enough: watchful-minded Penelope is\nless than you — slighter to look at, smaller —
for she is mortal, and you are deathless and unaging.
But even so I wish — and all my days I long —\nto go home, and to look upon my day of homecoming.
And if some god wrecks me again on the wine-dark sea,
I will endure it, with a heart\nschooled in enduring sorrows.
Much have I suffered already, much have I labored\nthrough waves and war. Let this be added to the rest."
So he spoke; and the sun went down, and the dusk came on;
and the two of them went into the inner hollow of the cave
and took their joy of love, and stayed side by side.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,\nstraightway Odysseus put on a cloak and tunic,
and she, the nymph, put on a great silver-shining mantle,
fine-woven and graceful, and cast about her waist a belt,
beautiful, golden, and set a veil on her head above.
Then she turned her mind to the\nsending of great-hearted Odysseus.
She gave him a great axe, fitted to his palms,\nof bronze, sharpened on both edges, and set in it
a beautiful handle of olive-wood, made firm and fast;\nthen she gave him a polished adze, and led the way
to the island's farthest edge, where the tall trees grew:
alder and black poplar, and fir that reached the sky,
long dry, dead-seasoned, that would ride for him lightly.
And when she had shown him where the tall trees grew,
Calypso went back to her house, shining among goddesses,
and he set to cutting timbers,\nand the work went quickly under him.
Twenty trees in all he felled,\nand trimmed them with the bronze,
and dressed them smooth with skill,\nand trued them to the line.
Meanwhile Calypso, shining\namong goddesses, brought augers,
and he bored through every piece and fitted each to each,\nand drove her together with pegs and joinery.
As wide as a man lays out the round of the hull of\na broad cargo ship — a man who knows his craft —
so wide Odysseus built his raft.
He set up half-decks, fitting them to close-set ribs,\nand finished with long gunwale planks.
He made a mast in her, and a yard fitted to it,\nand he made besides a steering-oar to hold her straight,
and fenced her round from stem\nto stern with plaited willow
to break the wave, and heaped down brush for ballast.
Meanwhile Calypso, shining among goddesses, brought\ncloth to make a sail; and he made that too, with craft,
and lashed into her the braces,\nthe halyards, and the sheets.
Then on rollers he hauled her\ndown to the bright salt water.
It was the fourth day, and all his work was done;\nand on the fifth shining Calypso sent him from the island,
having bathed him and dressed him in fragrant clothes.
And the goddess put a skin of dark wine aboard, one skin,\nand another, a great one, of water, and provisions
in a sack, and set in plenty of comforting meats;\nand she sent up a fair wind for him, harmless and warm.
Rejoicing in the wind, noble Odysseus spread his sail,
and with the steering-oar he steered her, craftsmanlike,\nsitting there; and sleep never fell on his eyelids
as he watched the Pleiades, and Boötes that sets late,
and the Bear, that men also call by the name of the Wagon,
who turns in her place and keeps her watch on Orion,\nand alone has no share in the baths of Ocean:
for Calypso, shining among goddesses, had told him\nto keep her on his left hand as he crossed the sea.
Seventeen days he sailed on, crossing the water,\nand on the eighteenth appeared the shadowy mountains
of the Phaeacians' land, where it lay nearest him:
it looked like a shield laid on the misted sea.
But the strong earth-shaker,\ncoming back from the Ethiopians,
saw him far off, from the\nmountains of the Solymi: he showed
to his eye, sailing the sea.\nAnd the god's heart grew the angrier,
and shaking his head he spoke to his own heart:
"Damnation! So the gods have changed their counsels\nabout Odysseus while I was among the Ethiopians —
and here he is, close to the Phaeacians' land,\nwhere it is his portion
to slip the great noose of misery that has come upon him.
But I say I will yet drive him deep enough in trouble."
So speaking he herded the clouds\ntogether, and stirred up the sea,
the trident in his hands; and he roused all the squalls
of every wind there is, and covered land and sea\nalike with cloud; and night rose up out of heaven.
East Wind and South fell on him together,\nand the hard-blowing West,
and the North Wind born of the\nclear sky, rolling a great wave.
And then Odysseus' knees went loose, and his heart;\nand deeply stirred he spoke to his own great heart:
"Ah, wretch that I am — what happens to me at the last?
I fear the goddess spoke it all unerringly,\nwho said that on the sea, before I reached my own country,
I would fill my measure of pains.\nNow it is all coming to pass:
look how Zeus crowns the wide heaven with cloud on cloud,
and has stirred up the sea, and the squalls of every wind
there is come driving.\nNow my sheer destruction is certain.
Three times blessed the Danaans, and four times, who died
in those years in wide Troy,\ndoing the Atreidae's pleasure!
Would that I too had died so, met my doom,\non the day the Trojans in their hundreds hurled
their bronze-tipped spears at\nme over the dead son of Peleus.
Then I would have had my death-rites,\nand the Achaeans carried my fame;
now it is my lot to be taken in a miserable death."
As he said it, a great wave drove down on him from\nabove, rushing terribly, and spun the raft around.
Far from the raft he fell, and the steering-oar\nflew from his hands; the mast snapped in the middle
under the terrible squall of winds meeting from all\nquarters, and sail and yard fell far off in the sea.
And the wave held him under a long time: he could not\nrise quickly from beneath the great sea's downrush,
for the clothes weighed on him that shining Calypso gave.
At long last he came up,\nspitting from his mouth the bitter
brine that ran streaming in torrents down his head.
Yet even so, ground down as he was,\nhe did not forget his raft:
he lunged after her through the waves and caught hold,
and sat down in the middle of her,\ndodging the end that is death,
while the great wave carried her\nwith the current, here and there.
As when the North Wind of autumn carries thistledown
across the plain, and the tufts\ncling close to one another,
so the winds carried her over\nthe open water, here and there:
now the South Wind would toss her to the North to carry,
now again the East would yield her to the West to chase.
But the daughter of Cadmus saw him —\nIno of the beautiful ankles,
the White Goddess, who once was\nmortal, with a mortal voice,
and now in the salt depths has\nher share of honor from the gods.
She pitied Odysseus, driven wandering, worn with pains,
and in the likeness of a shearwater\nshe rose on the wing from the water,
and perched on the close-bound raft, and said:
"Luckless man, why is Poseidon the earth-shaker
so terribly at odds with you,\nthat he plants all these evils for you?
Yet he shall not destroy you, for all his fury.
Only do exactly this —\nyou do not seem to me short of sense.
Strip off these clothes, and leave the raft for the winds
to carry; strike out swimming\nwith your hands for a homecoming
on the Phaeacians' land,\nwhere it is your portion to escape.
Here — spread this veil under your chest.
It is immortal: no fear then of suffering or death.
But the moment your hands take hold of dry land,\nuntie it again and throw it into the wine-dark sea,
far out from land, and turn your own face away."
So speaking the goddess gave him the veil,\nand she herself sank back into the surging sea
in the likeness of a shearwater,\nand the black wave closed over her.
But much-enduring noble Odysseus pondered,\nand deeply stirred he spoke to his own great heart:
"Ah me — let this not be some new snare of the immortals\nwoven against me, when she bids me abandon my raft.
No: I will not obey her yet. Far off with my own\neyes I saw the land where she said my refuge is.
I will do this instead — it seems to me the best:
as long as the timbers hold in their fastenings,\nso long I stay aboard and endure my sufferings where I am;
but the moment the wave shakes the raft to pieces,\nI swim. There is no better plan to see."
While he was turning this over\nin his mind and in his heart,
Poseidon the earth-shaker heaved up a great wave,\nterrible and grim, arching over him, and drove it down.
And as a violent wind tosses a heap of dry chaff\nand scatters the wisps this way and that way,
so it scattered the raft's long timbers. But Odysseus\ngot astride one beam, like a man riding a racehorse,
and stripped off the clothes that shining Calypso gave,\nand spread the veil at once beneath his chest,
and plunged headfirst in the sea, arms spread wide,\nhungry to swim. And the strong earth-shaker saw him,
and shaking his head he spoke to his own heart:
"So — now suffer your many evils and drift the sea,\nuntil you come among a people nurtured of Zeus.
But even so I do not think you\nwill make light of your trouble."
So speaking he lashed his horses of the beautiful\nmanes and came to Aegae, where his famous house is.
But Athena, daughter of Zeus, thought of other things.
She bound up the courses of all the other winds\nand commanded every one to rest and fall asleep,
and roused the quick North Wind,\nand broke the waves before him,
so that Zeus-born Odysseus might come among the oar-loving
Phaeacians, having slipped past death and the dooms.
Two nights then and two days on the close-packed swell
he drifted, and many times his heart\nlooked destruction in the face.
But when Dawn of the lovely braids\nbrought the third day round,
then at last the wind fell, and a windless\ncalm came on; and he saw the land close by,
casting a sharp glance forward, lifted on a great wave.
As when a father's life shows\ndear and welcome to his children —
a father who lies in sickness suffering strong pains,\nlong wasting away, some hateful power upon him,
and then, dear and welcome,\nthe gods set him free of his evil —
so welcome to Odysseus showed the land and the trees,
and he swam hard, straining to set foot on solid earth.
But when he was as far offshore as a man's shout carries,\nhe heard the boom of sea against the rock-teeth:
the great swell thundered on the dry land's edge,
belching terribly, and everything\nwas shrouded in salt spray.
For there were no harbors there\nto hold ships, no roadsteads —
only jutting headlands, rock-teeth, and cliff-faces.
And then Odysseus' knees went loose, and his heart,\nand deeply stirred he spoke to his own great heart:
"Ah me — now that Zeus has given me sight of land\nunhoped for, and I have won across this gulf at last,
no way out of the gray salt water shows anywhere:
sharp crags offshore, and all around them the wave\nroaring and churning, and the rock running up sheer,
and the sea deep close in — nowhere to\nstand on both my feet and escape the evil.
If I try to climb out, the great wave may snatch me
and hurl me on the standing stone,\nand my try go for nothing.
But if I swim along still farther, hoping to find\nshelving beaches somewhere, and harbors of the sea,
I fear the storm-squall snatches me up again and carries me,\ngroaning heavily, over the fish-filled sea —
or some power looses a monster on me out of the brine,\none of the swarm that famous Amphitrite pastures:
for I know how the famous shaker\nof earth is at odds with me."
While he was turning this over in his mind and in his heart,\na great wave carried him onto the jagged shore.
There his skin would have been\nstripped, his bones smashed in,
had not the goddess, gray-eyed\nAthena, put a thought in him:
lunging in, he seized the rock with both hands and\nclung there groaning while the great wave went past.
That one he escaped so; but its backwash leapt on him\nagain and struck him and threw him far out to sea.
As when an octopus is dragged out of its den\nand thick pebbles cling in the cups of its arms,
so from his bold hands the skin was stripped away\nagainst the rocks; and the great wave closed over him.
There, before his time,\nwretched Odysseus would have perished,
had not gray-eyed Athena given him clear sense.
Coming up out of the surf where it belches at the land,
he swam along outside it,\nlooking to the shore in hope of finding
shelving beaches somewhere, and harbors of the sea.
But when, swimming, he came to\nthe mouth of a fair-flowing river,
there at last the ground seemed best to him,\nclear of stones, and there was shelter from the wind.
He felt the current flowing and prayed in his heart:
"Hear me, lord, whoever you are.\nI come to you — the much-prayed-to —
a fugitive out of the sea, from the threats of Poseidon.
Even to the deathless gods that man is\nsacred who comes as a wanderer, as I come now
to your stream and to your knees, after much labor.
Pity me, lord: I declare myself your suppliant."
And at once the god stayed his\ncurrent, held back the wave,
and made the water calm before him, and brought him\nsafe into the river's mouth. And he bent both knees
and let his strong hands fall:\nthe sea had crushed the heart in him.
All his flesh was swollen, and the sea oozed in streams
up through his mouth and nostrils.\nBreathless and speechless
he lay, barely alive,\nand a terrible weariness came over him.
But when he got his breath again,\nand the spirit gathered in his chest,
then he unbound the goddess's veil from his body\nand let it go into the river running seaward,
and the great wave carried it back\ndown the current, and quickly Ino
took it in her own dear hands.\nAnd he turned from the river,
sank down in the reeds, and kissed the grain-giving earth;
and deeply stirred he spoke to his own great heart:
"Ah me, what now? What happens to me at the last?
If I keep watch through the\nanxious night here by the river,
the two together — the evil frost and the soaking dew —\nmay finish me: weak as I am, my spirit gasping;
and toward dawn a cold breeze blows off a river.
But if I climb the slope to the shadowy wood and\nfall asleep in the thick brush — supposing cold
and weariness release me, and sweet sleep comes —\nI fear I become spoil and carrion for wild beasts."
Yet as he weighed it, this seemed the better way:
he went up toward the wood, and found it near the water
on a rise in the open. He crept in under a double thicket
grown from a single stock —\none wild olive, one the planted tree.
Through these no strength of\nwet-blowing winds could pierce,
nor could the shining sun strike through with its rays,\nnor rain soak through them, so close they grew,
laced into one another. Under these Odysseus\ncrept, and heaped himself at once a wide bed
with his own hands: for there was a drift of fallen\nleaves there, deep, enough to shelter two men or three
in the winter season, however hard it blew.
Seeing it, much-enduring noble Odysseus rejoiced,
and he lay down in the middle and\npoured the fallen leaves over him.
As when a man buries a burning log in a black ash-heap
at the far edge of the fields —\na man with no neighbors near —
saving the seed of fire,\nso as not to seek a light elsewhere,
so Odysseus buried himself in the leaves.\nAnd Athena poured sleep upon his eyes, to free him soonest
from his toil-worn weariness,\nwhen she had folded his dear eyelids shut.
